summary_paraphrase: Alex feels unwell and his mother takes him to Dr Bongi, who gives him medicine. He finds medicine yucky and tries to avoid it: he offers Jett his toy car to drink it, pours it on a sandwich, buries it in the garden and hides it in a bird's nest. Each plan fails. At last he wonders whether to just try it; the medicine turns into an imagined green sea he rides, and he feels much better while his family says they are proud.

humor_notes: OBSERVED: the humor is a pattern of three failed schemes, each set up on an idea spread and knocked down on the next by one interjection and a picture (goo-drowned sandwich, dog with the bottle, bird kicking it out). The text alone does not say how any plan failed.

repetition.description: an idea spread (thinking face with question marks, then a lightbulb page with 'I know, I'll ...') followed by a failure spread (one interjection on a lime page, the result on white)
repetition.why: after the first round the listener predicts the failure and can say the cry; the layout itself (yellow bulb, lime cry) signals the pattern
a joinable cue that marks each new scheme

repetition.description: every object from the failed plans floats in the medicine sea
repetition.why: gathers the book's failures into the payoff picture

notes: OBSERVED: each failure (pages 5, 7, 9) is a single-word cry in the text; what went wrong is shown only in the picture.
OBSERVED: colour codes the pattern: yellow lightbulb pages for ideas, lime pages for the shocked cry.
OBSERVED: the text never says who gives the dose; page 10 shows Mom giving it on a spoon.
OBSERVED: the dog and the bird that foil the plans are not in the text.
OBSERVED: the 'super' of the title is a red cape drawn on Alex at the end and on the bottle in the cover and closing vignette; the text never mentions a cape.
OBSERVED: all dialogue is untagged; speakers are shown by speech and thought bubbles.

strengths: a clear pattern of three attempts with a predictable, joinable failure beat
failures are funny and land in the picture, letting the text stay to one word
the child decides to try; the change is his
the final imagined sea gathers every earlier plan
very short sentences suited to a young listener
weaknesses: the health message is stated at the end (all I had to do was drink my medicine)
the bribe asks another child to drink his medicine, presented as a joke without comment
the speaker of untagged lines depends on the bubbles; read aloud without pictures several lines are ambiguous
medicine is shown as instantly transformative

anti_patterns.note: the last line states the lesson after the picture has already shown it

age_suitability.notes: Medicine content. OBSERVED: the child hides prescribed medicine (pours it on food, buries it, puts it in a nest) and offers it to another child in exchange for a toy; a dog carries the bottle in its mouth. These are imitable and two are medication-safety risks (another child drinking it, a pet reaching it); the book frames them as failed jokes, never says they are unsafe. On the positive side the picture shows an adult giving the dose on a spoon. Any MagicPaper use should keep medicine in adult hands, drop the swap with another child and keep animals away from it. Peak research intensity 4 of 5 (the ruined sandwich and the imagined sea), about 2 on the engine's 0-3 scale; illness itself stays at 2 of 5, about 1 on the 0-3 scale; no fear of illness or of the doctor. 139 words, mean sentence 5.4, longest 15: fits 3-4 as read-aloud, also 5-6. Text-only MagicPaper would lose the failures, which live in the pictures.
